Unreal Engine 4 is the first major game engine to provide official Vulkan support.

It's my understanding that Vulkan, while better all around than OpenGL is also harder to work with, something about "With great power something responsibility". Anyways, does the game engines including Vulkan renderers abstract all that for the game developers and make it easier to get efficient results?

Anyways, does the game engines including Vulkan renderers abstract all that for the game developers and make it easier to get efficient results?

Assuming they use something like UnrealEngine or Unity...yea. Otherwise, to the coal mines!

I spent this past weekend getting into the Vulkan API, and honestly...it's not THAT much more difficult. If you wanted OpenGL or dx11 to run well, you'd have to be doing crazy stuff anyway. The biggest difference is that Vulkan is a lot more explicit and much wordier. But once you get all the boilerplate stuff out of the way, it won't require god-like programming skills...just not indie game dev skills.

One of the ways Vulkan is able to perform better is by reducing the driver error checking over head, and by giving the developer access closer to the metal of the GPU, so yeah it's harder to work with because you need to manage much more that drivers used to be doing. Most gameplay developers using large engines (Unreal, Unity, CryEngine) never have to deal with the low level specifics in the engine, Engine developers are the ones who have to wade through all of the low level code. So yes most developers will be able to take advantage of the new efficiency without much change to their existing workflow.
